chicken-thigh-baked-broiled-or-roasted-s.title: Chicken thigh, baked, broiled, or roasted, skin not eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Skinless chicken thigh is meat from the upper leg of the bird, prepared by baking, broiling or roasting. Removing the skin reduces fat content while preserving the rich flavor and juiciness of the meat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Thigh meat contains more iron than chicken breast because of higher myoglobin levels.
During dry‑heat cooking, melted fat and Maillard reactions create aromatic compounds that enhance taste.
Chicken thighs are a staple in many cuisines: American BBQ, Indian curries, and Russian “Kurochka po‑derevenski” stews.
The edible portion is about 70 % of the raw weight; the rest is bone and connective tissue.
Proper cooking requires an internal temperature of 165 °F (74 °C) to kill harmful bacteria.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Skinless thigh provides roughly 22 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 aids amino‑acid metabolism and nervous‑system function.

items.title: Contains zinc
items.content: Zinc is essential for immune health and wound healing.

items.title: Lower fat than skin‑on cuts
items.content: Removing the skin cuts saturated‑fat intake, making it suitable for lower‑fat diets.

items.title: Provides selenium
items.content: Selenium acts as an antioxidant and supports thyroid function.

items.title: Risk of foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked chicken may harbor Salmonella or Campylobacter; cook to an internal 74 °C.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals are allergic to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium in marinades
items.content: Marinated thighs can be high in sodium, which may be a concern for hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Skinless thighs can be baked, pan‑seared, or grilled. They pair well with herbs (rosemary, thyme), spices (paprika, garlic) and marinades based on yogurt or lemon juice. Serve with vegetables, whole grains, or sliced in salads.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh thighs keep in the refrigerator at +2–4 °C for up to 2 days. Frozen thighs are safe for up to 9 months at ‑18 °C. Thaw frozen meat in the fridge, not at room temperature. Cooked thighs stored in an airtight container last about 3 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Corn pone, baked is a traditional American bread made from cornmeal, milk, eggs, and a small amount of sugar. The batter is baked until a golden crust forms, yielding a dense yet slightly crumbly texture with a distinctive corn aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Corn pone originated in colonial America as a simple way to use locally grown cornmeal.
It was traditionally cooked in iron skillets or on stone griddles over an open fire.
In some regions it is nicknamed “Indian bread,” although the original recipe differs from Native American dishes.
During the early 20th century it became a staple of Southern home cooking.
Corn pone is often served with honey, butter, or jam.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Cornmeal provides slow‑releasing energy, helping to maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: B1, B3 and B5 vitamins aid carbohydrate metabolism and support the nervous system.

items.title: Provides magnesium and iron
items.content: These minerals are important for muscle function and blood formation.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Unlike many baked goods, corn pone is low in fat when no additional oil is added.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to corn products.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Cornmeal can raise blood sugar quickly, so people with diabetes should consume it in moderation.

items.title: Gluten content
items.content: The traditional recipe is gluten‑free, but adding wheat flour introduces gluten, which is a concern for those with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Corn pone can be enjoyed warm, sliced and spread with butter, honey, or jam. It is commonly served alongside soups, stews, or as part of a breakfast plate with eggs and bacon.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store baked corn pone in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer storage, refrigerate (up to 5 days) or freeze, tightly wrapped in plastic.

content.title: About
content.content: Creamy Italian dressing, fat free is a low‑fat salad dressing made with skimmed yogurt and reduced‑fat cheese powder, flavored with classic Italian herbs, garlic and spices. It delivers a rich, creamy texture and the familiar tang of Italian dressing without the added fat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Fat‑free creamy dressings are popular among calorie‑conscious consumers because they keep the mouthfeel of full‑fat versions.
Italian herbs such as basil, oregano and rosemary give the dressing its distinctive Mediterranean aroma.
The skimmed yogurt base provides live probiotic cultures that support gut health.
It can be used on salads, pasta, fish, and chicken as a lighter alternative to traditional creamy dressings.
In the United States the product is often marketed to people following low‑fat or weight‑management diets.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The near‑zero fat content makes it suitable for low‑fat and reduced‑calorie eating plans.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Skimmed yogurt and cheese powder contribute a modest amount of protein.

items.title: Contains probiotics
items.content: Live cultures from the yogurt can help maintain a healthy intestinal microbiome.

items.title: Rich in vitamins and minerals
items.content: Herbs and dairy ingredients provide vitamin A, calcium and magnesium.

items.title: May aid blood‑sugar control
items.content: Low carbohydrate and fat levels make it a friendly option for people monitoring blood glucose.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: The product contains dairy, which can cause discomfort for those who are lactose intolerant.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: People allergic to milk proteins (casein, whey) should avoid it.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some formulations may have added salt; individuals with hypertension should watch portion size.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: The dressing may contain preservatives that some consumers prefer to avoid.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use the dressing as a salad topping, stir it into pasta, drizzle over roasted vegetables, marinate chicken or fish, or spread on sandwiches as a low‑fat alternative to mayo.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at 1 °C–4 °C. Once opened, consume within 7–10 days. Do not freeze, as the texture may separate.

content.title: About
content.content: An egg sandwich on biscuit is a quick breakfast or snack consisting of a soft biscuit, a fried egg, and often additions such as cheese, ham, or vegetables. The biscuit gives a tender, slightly sweet texture while the egg provides protein and a rich flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Using a biscuit as the base is popular in the Southern United States, where it’s often called an “egg biscuit.”
The classic version features a runny‑yolk egg so the yolk lightly drips.
Variations may include ranch sauce, avocado, or hot sauce for extra kick.
Biscuit dough is frequently made with buttermilk, making it extra fluffy.
Egg sandwich on biscuit is a staple in fast‑food chains and coffee shops as a “breakfast sandwich.”

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Eggs provide a complete source of protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs contain vitamin B12, riboflavin, and folate, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Source of choline
items.content: Choline in the yolk is important for brain function and liver health.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Eggs offer easily absorbable iron, helpful for preventing anemia.

items.title: Moderate healthy fats
items.content: The yolk supplies monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats that support heart health.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to egg whites.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Egg yolks contain cholesterol; people with high cholesterol should consume in moderation.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The biscuit and added toppings (cheese, ham) can increase the calorie count.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked eggs may harbor salmonella; cook eggs thoroughly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sandwich is usually split in half and eaten by hand. It can be topped with fresh veggies, lettuce, sauce, or mustard for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Best enjoyed fresh. If needed, store in the refrigerator in an airtight container for up to 24 hours; reheat in a microwave or toaster before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Tilapia is a freshwater fish from the cichlid family, widely farmed in aquaculture. The NFS (1117) strain is a popular commercial variety known for its mild flavor, tender white flesh, and low fat content.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tilapia is one of the fastest‑growing farmed fish, reaching market size in 6‑8 months.
Unlike many marine species, tilapia can thrive on plant‑based feeds, reducing production costs.
It can be raised in both fresh and slightly brackish water conditions.
The flesh is virtually boneless, making it convenient for children and people with chewing difficulties.
Tilapia is featured in cuisines worldwide, from Asian to Mediterranean dishes.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Tilapia contains less fat than many other fish, making it suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: A 100‑g serving provides about 20 g of high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It supplies vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, which support energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Tilapia provides phosphorus, selenium, and potassium, important for bones, antioxidant protection, and blood pressure regulation.

items.title: Moderate omega‑3
items.content: While lower in omega‑3 than fatty fish, tilapia still contributes to cardiovascular health.

items.title: Contaminants from low‑quality feed
items.content: If raised on feed containing excessive chemicals, harmful residues may accumulate in the flesh.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fish, including tilapia.

items.title: Low omega‑3 content
items.content: For those seeking high omega‑3 levels, tilapia is not a substitute for fatty fish like salmon.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Tilapia can be baked, grilled, steamed, or poached. It pairs well with lemon, herbs, garlic, and light sauces. Boneless fillets are easy to cube for salads, soups, and tacos.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh tilapia refrigerated at 0‑2 °C and use within 2 days. Frozen fillets store at –18 °C for up to 6 months. Rinse and pat dry before cooking.

content.title: About
content.content: Mole is a traditional Mexican sauce first produced commercially in 1924. It blends more than 20 ingredients, including chilies, chocolate, spices, nuts, and dried fruit, creating a complex, slightly sweet and spicy flavor. The sauce is commonly served with meat, poultry, and vegetables.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first industrial mole recipe was created in Mexico City in 1924 and quickly gained popularity in the United States.
There are over 20 regional mole variations, each with its own spice blend and proportions.
Traditional mole can contain up to 30 ingredients, often featuring pumpkin seeds, almonds, and raisins.
Mole is frequently prepared for special dishes such as mole poblano and black mole.
The original recipe used Mexican chocolate, giving the sauce its distinctive aroma.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: The cocoa and spices provide antioxidant protection for cells.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Nuts and seeds supply beneficial monounsaturated fats.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Chilies and whole grains deliver vitamin B6 and niacin, important for metabolism.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Almonds and pumpkin seeds add magnesium, iron, and zinc.

items.title: Moderate fiber content
items.content: Dried fruit and nuts aid digestion.

items.title: Nut and seed allergies
items.content: The sauce may contain almonds, pumpkin seeds, and other allergens.

items.title: High sodium level
items.content: Some mole varieties contain a notable amount of salt, which can be an issue for hypertension.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Because of nuts and chocolate, mole is fairly calorie‑dense; portion control is advised.

items.title: Spicy capsaicin content
items.content: Chilies make the sauce hot, which may irritate sensitive stomachs.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve mole hot over roasted meat, chicken, turkey, or vegetables. It can be added to marinades, used as a taco sauce, or drizzled over rice. For a milder taste, thin the sauce with broth.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep mole in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 weeks. For longer storage, freeze in portions for up to 3 months. Allow the sauce to reach room temperature before use.

content.title: About
content.content: Veal chop is a cut of meat from a young calf (usually 3–6 months old), taken from the loin or rib section. The meat is light pink, tender, with a mild flavor and relatively low fat content.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Veal is considered a leaner meat compared with beef because of its lower fat content.
Veal chops are featured in classic French and Italian dishes such as "Veal Milanese" and "Veal Piccata".
Because the meat is tender, it cooks quickly – pan‑searing, grilling, or baking to medium doneness keeps it juicy.
In some countries calves are raised on milk‑based diets, which gives the meat a delicate taste.
Veal is rich in heme iron, making it an excellent source of easily absorbable iron.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Veal provides complete protein needed for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with beef, veal contains less saturated fat, which is better for heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: B‑vitamin complex
items.content: It supplies vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, essential for energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Iron and zinc
items.content: The heme iron in veal is readily absorbed, and zinc supports immunity and wound healing.

items.title: Creatine source
items.content: Veal naturally contains creatine, which can help improve muscle strength and endurance.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked veal may harbor harmful bacteria such as Salmonella. Cook to an internal temperature of at least 63 °C (145 °F).

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Rarely, individuals may experience allergic reactions to meat proteins.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: Like other red meats, veal contains purines, which can exacerbate gout symptoms.

items.title: Hormones and antibiotics
items.content: Choose certified products to avoid residues of growth hormones or antibiotics.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Veal chops can be pan‑seared, grilled, or baked. Lightly pounding the chop ensures even thickness. Serve with vegetable sides, wine‑based sauces, or creamy reductions. Thinly sliced veal works well in salads and sandwiches.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep veal refrigerated at 0‑4 °C and use within 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze in an airtight bag at –18 °C for up to 6 months. Thaw in the refrigerator, not at room temperature, before cooking.

content.title: About
content.content: Watercress (Nasturtium officinale) is a fast‑growing aquatic leafy plant widely used in cooking. When cooked it retains a mildly peppery flavor and a pleasant crunch, making it a popular addition to soups, stews, omelets and side dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Watercress grows in clean, flowing freshwater and is an indicator of water quality.
It contains 5‑6 times more vitamin C than an orange per gram of fresh weight.
Ancient Romans used it as a remedy for colds and to aid digestion.
Watercress belongs to the cruciferous family, alongside broccoli and cabbage.
Heat treatment reduces some of its bitterness while softening the aroma.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C boosts immunity and is essential for collagen synthesis, supporting skin and blood‑vessel health.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Beta‑carotene, lutein and zeaxanthin in watercress protect cells from oxidative damage.

items.title: Supports bone health
items.content: Calcium and vitamin K help maintain strong bones and proper blood clotting.

items.title: Low‑calorie protein source
items.content: Cooked watercress retains a modest amount of plant protein, useful for vegetarian diets.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: Fiber and bitter compounds stimulate bile production, improving fat digestion.

items.title: Water contamination
items.content: The plant can accumulate bacteria and heavy metals from polluted water; thorough washing and cooking are recommended.

items.title: Thyroid interaction
items.content: Glucosinolates may affect thyroid function if consumed in very large amounts.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: A small number of people may experience an allergy to cruciferous vegetables.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Watercress is typically blanched for 1‑2 minutes, then quickly sautéed or added at the end of cooking to preserve its bright color and flavor. It works well in soups, pasta, omelets, and as a garnish for meat or fish dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh watercress in the refrigerator in a sealed container lined with a damp paper towel, and use within 3‑4 days. Cooked watercress should be stored in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 2 days.
